entries.title: Germany news: EU ministers meet for migration showdown
entries.summary: European interior ministers hold migration talks in Munich as the bloc plans to strengthen borders and speed up deportations. Meanwhile, trade unions staged nationwide demos against health and welfare cuts. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: EU ministers meet for migration showdown

Published September 26, 2026last updated September 26, 2026

European interior ministers hold migration talks in Munich as the bloc plans to strengthen borders and speed up deportations. Meanwhile, trade unions staged nationwide demos against health and welfare cuts. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • European interior ministers gather in Munich to tighten EU migration policy
  • Germany's Olympic committee decides Munich will bid to host the Games in 2036, 2040 or 2044
  • Trade unions stage protests in 15 cities against health, welfare cuts
  • Former Chancellor Angela Merkel, a Protestant, wins top Catholic charity's prize

Follow our blog for the latest news and analysis from across Germany for the weekend of September 26-27, 2026.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Germany Olympic bid: Munich named candidate city

Germany Olympic bid: Munich named candidate city

The German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) announced on Saturday that Munich has been chosen as Germany's candidate city to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics in either 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The Bavarian capital beat a rival Cologne-led bid from the western Rhine-Ruhr region.

Berlin had withdrawn its bid earlier in the week, while the residents of Hamburg voted against a bid in a referendum earlier this year.

Skip next section Mass protests against cuts to social services

Mass protests against cuts to social services

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets of cities across Germany on Saturday to voice their opposition to planned government spending cuts and call for a stronger welfare state.

Trade unions said a total of 175,000 took part in the protests, including in Nuremberg (over 20,000), Stuttgart (16,000), Frankfurt (15,000), Hanover (13,000), Essen (12,000), Berlin (5,500) and elsewhere under the slogan: "Hard-earned! Your work. Your health. Your pension."

Speaking in the western city of Essen, German Trade Union Confederation (DGB) leader Yasmin Fahimi criticized plans by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition government to reform working hours and pensions, and warned against cuts to social security benefits.

"We will not simply allow what we have built up over many years in terms of social standards to be taken away from us," she said.

Pension reform has been the focus of attention for months in Germany, while automobile giant Volkswagen has also announced sweeping job cuts.

The issues played a central role in the recent state elections in Berlin and the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, which resulted in disastrous defeats for Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Nevertheless, the chancellor insisted earlier this month: "The reforms must go ahead."

Christiane Benner, leader of the trade union IG Metall, warned in Nuremberg against scaling back social security in times of restructuring and job cuts, for example in the automotive sector.

"Economic change can only succeed with confidence in the future and with solidarity," she said.

German employers, however, accused the trade unions of a "ritual refusal to reform."

Steffen Kampeter, chief executive of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), told the DPA news agency that "the trade unions say 'no' to almost every change" and accused them of "dreaming of the world of yesterday."

Skip next section Migration: Dobrindt calls for expanded Frontex role

Migration: Dobrindt calls for expanded Frontex role

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has called for an "expanded mandate" for the European Union's border protection agency Frontex when it comes to the deportation of illegal migrants.

"We are of the belief that we can strengthen the use of Frontex in deportation cases," he said ahead of a meeting of EU interior ministers in Munich on Saturday, calling for Frontex's area of operation to be expanded to "transit countries" outside the bloc.

"Of course, only with the agreement of these countries," he added.

Dobrindt said he also wanted to expand Frontex's responsibilities to "Dublin Regulations" – referring to the rules which determine which EU member state is responsible for the processing of an asylum application.

"A new European migration mechanism is needed," he said.

Skip next section Police close 2 autobahns to free giant wind-turbine

Police close 2 autobahns to free giant wind-turbine

A wide-load truck carrying a nearly 100-meter-long (328-feet-long) wind turbine blade forced the closure of two motorways in western Germany after it got stuck along a narrow section of the carriageway.

The daily Bild newspaper reported that the truck was traveling along the A43 autobahn near the Recklinghausen interchange in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia when the dramatic incident unfolded on Wednesday evening.

Police said the driver ignored warning signs that the highway was unsuitable for heavy-load vehicles.

"The highway is not permitted for heavy transport vehicles in that area. They have to exit because the route crosses the Rhine-Herne Canal a little further on," a spokesperson for Münster Police's highway patrol told Bild.

An automatic barrier and weighing system is meant to prevent loads over 3.5 tons from crossing an old bridge over the canal.

After initially blocking traffic on A43, the truck was ordered onto the hard shoulder to allow traffic to restart along one remaining open lane.

The police spokesperson said "several attempts" were made to free the truck with its ultra-wide cargo over the next two days.

On Friday night, the driver agreed to reverse his truck onto the nearby A2, which forced the temporary closure of a second autobahn, before being allowed to continue his journey just after midnight on Saturday.

Skip next section Rail services canceled, delayed after suspected cable theft

Rail services canceled, delayed after suspected cable theft

Police blamed disruption to high-speed rail services in western Germany on deliberate damage to signal cabling overnight.

National rail operator Deutsche Bahn said trains running between Dortmund and Munich, Hamburg and Basel, and northern Germany and Cologne faced cancellations, delays and diversions.

According to the Zuginfo.nrw website, the entire Gelsenkirchen metropolitan area is currently impassable.

A police spokesman said officers were investigating suspected cable theft on a railway line in Gelsenkirchen-Ückendorf, where signals and control systems had failed.

The suspects are believed to have crudely cut and ripped out cables beside the tracks at several points.

It is unclear how long the repair work will take.

Skip next section Caritas honors Merkel with prize for social cohesion

Caritas honors Merkel with prize for social cohesion

Former Chancellor Angela Merkel, a Protestant, received one of the highest honors of the Catholic Church's social welfare charity in Germany.

The 72-year-old was awarded the Elisabeth Prize by the Catholic Caritas Association at an event in the southern city of Augsburg on Friday evening.

The prize is named after Saint Elizabeth of Thuringia, who lived from 1207 to 1231 and who helped people in need. She is the patron saint of Caritas.

The honor recognized Merkel's commitment to social cohesion, with Caritas President Eva Welskop-Deffaa paying tribute to the "inner compass with which she [Merkel] successfully steered the country's fortunes."

The former chancellor told the roughly 400 guests that "there will always be a need for people to be there for one another."

Once seen by some as Mutti — Germany’s reassuring mother figure — Merkel has become an increasingly divisive figure because of her 2015 decision to open the borders to more than a million refugees.

Critics say Merkel’s decision fueled years of backlash that helped turn the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from a fringe protest party into a force that now leads most national polls.

Skip next section Dobrindt seeks 'hardening' of EU borders at Munich talks

Dobrindt seeks 'hardening' of EU borders at Munich talks

Several European Union interior ministers are meeting in Munich this afternoon to discuss tightening the bloc's migration policy.

A spokesperson for German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the Münchner Merkur newspaper that the talks will focus on the "implementation of a shift in migration policy."

The 17 ministers will discuss "further refining the European Migration Pact, consistently hardening the European Union's external borders, and accelerating returns from Europe," the spokesperson added.

Germany and Denmark, Austria, the Netherlands, and Greece are due to hold separate talks about the creation of deportation centers or return hubs in third countries.

Germany hopes to secure a deal with a country in Africa or possibly Asia by the end of the year.

Dobrindt's spokesperson said the EU's border agency, Frontex, could be turned into a "border protection and genuine return agency."

Currently, EU member states are responsible for returning asylum seekers whose applications have failed.

EU Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner will also attend the Munich talks.

Skip next section Munich or Cologne: Germany set to pick Olympic bid city

Munich or Cologne: Germany set to pick Olympic bid city

Germany's Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) will reveal at lunchtime which city will bid to host a future Olympic Games.

After the capital, Berlin, withdrew earlier this week, the vote will be a two-horse race  between Munich and Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr to be the candidate city for either the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Games.

Germany is keeping its options open regarding which Games to bid for, as the 2036 Olympics is widely expected to go to an Asian country.

The year 2036 is also politically sensitive as it would mark 100 years since Berlin hosted the 1936 Olympics during the Nazi era.

Some policymakers want Germany to bid for 2040, as it will mark 50 years since German reunification.

If it wins, Munich plans to host most Olympic events within city limits and already has stadia and other sports infrastructure in place, including the Olympic Park, which was built for the 1972 Games.

Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr plans to spread the Games across several cities, including Schalke for swimming events, Düsseldorf for basketball and football at Borussia Dortmund's 81,000-seat stadium.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from DW. In Munich, you'll often hear Grüss Gott (greet God), while in Cologne and Germany's Rhine-Ruhr region, people often say Tachchen (Hey there).

It's decision day for both cities as Germany's Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) picks which one will bid to host the Olympic Games in 2036, 2040, or 2044.

Munich will also be hosting European interior ministers for talks on implementing a tougher EU migration policy.

Fifteen other cities, including Berlin, Hamburg and Nuremberg, will stage protests against the government's planned cuts to the social welfare bill.

We'll bring you updates on these and other top news stories from across Germany throughout the day.

entries.title: Backlash over data centers tests Europe's AI ambitions
entries.summary: Massive data centers needed to run AI are triggering protests across Europe. Their operators counter that they boost digital sovereignty and energy independence.
entries.content:
September 26, 2026

Massive data centers needed to run AI are triggering protests across Europe. Their operators counter that they boost digital sovereignty and energy independence.

Like coal-fired power plants and wind turbines, few people actually want a data center in their backyard. But they do want to use their services. As a global debate rages about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence, there are also many local discussions about where exactly the data centers needed to train and run AI should be built.

This is currently a major issue in Europe, where many governments and companies have decided that they would prefer to store data in Europe rather than in the United States, which is the global leader in computing. But more digital sovereignty in Europe will mean more consumption of the continent's resources.

According to the German Ministry for Economic Affairs, for every kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed, an average of between 0.4 and 4.4 liters (0.8 and 9.3 pints) of water is used to cool data centers, with the water either evaporating or being diverted back to tanks in a warmed state.

Massive water consumption

The summer that just ended was the hottest on record in Europe — in some areas, water use was restricted for residents, agriculture and even nuclear power plants. The summers are expected to get warmer, so many are wondering about the potential water consumption of data centers in the future.

They are also worried about the high electricity consumption of the centers. Fingrid, Finland's national grid operator, recently forecast that electricity consumption would rise by almost 40% if all projects with signed connection agreements were implemented in full.

This week, the European Commission announced a new scheme for data centers to increase transparency on their energy and water use. Those with a capacity of more than 500 kW will receive an efficiency grade that will also take into account their contribution to the grid, such as the reuse of waste heat. "Tripling our data center capacity cannot mean tripling the pressure on our grids, our water and our energy bills," said  Teresa Ribera, the Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for a Clean, Just and Competitive Transition.

Data centers in urban hubs and rural areas

Europe's most powerful data centers have primarily been built near the major cities of Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin (FLAP-D) because of high connectivity, proximity to users and businesses, and well-established ecosystems with specialized engineers and secure supply chains.

However, according to a report by the investment group CBRE, the situation is changing as these markets face power and grid infrastructure constraints. New data centers are being built in the Dutch city of Groningen, Barcelona in Spain or the Belgian capital Brussels, as well as in more rural areas.

And as this happens, there are more and more protests taking place, both on and offline. Earlier this month, hundreds turned up for a protest in front of tech giant Google's offices in the Austrian city of Linz, demonstrating against its already advanced plans to build a data center in the small town of Kronstorf.

Earlier this month, bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney successfully led a campaign to overturn planning permission for a proposed data center in the village of Killala, arguing that it would breach national climate policy.

In central France, meanwhile, several elected officials in the village of Etrechet have resigned over Google's plans to build a massive data center, which, at full capacity, would require between 880 megawatts and 1.1 gigawatts of electricity or the equivalent of the total output of a nuclear power plant. Etrechet mayor Florence Laurent told the French daily Le Monde that she was resigning out of a "sense of powerlessness, since the village has no decision-making power" regarding the project.

Some operators of data centers argue that the facilities can be built in such a way that they save energy. A large data center currently being built in Marseille will reportedly use a cooling system that requires 30% less power and consumes no water.

Other data centers, in Scandinavia, for example, use waste heat from the servers and route it into district heating networks via heat exchangers and pumps.

This spring, the German energy company E.ON published the results of a survey that found nearly three-quarters of people would be more likely to welcome data centers near residential areas if they fed their waste heat into the heating network.

Data center operators also argue that the facilities can serve the public by connecting the batteries that usually provide backup power to local grids so that there is uninterrupted service in the event of power outages or at times of peak demand.

For proponents of building more data centers in Europe, the facilities not only contribute to the continent's digital sovereignty but also help to strengthen energy independence.

Monir Ghaedi contributed to this article, which was translated from German.

entries.title: China, US agree to set up channel for AI safety incidents
entries.summary: Following the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the two superpowers pledged to set up a "communication channel" for AI incidents and boost coordination on military matters.
entries.content:
September 26, 2026

Following the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the two superpowers pledged to set up a "communication channel" for AI incidents and boost coordination on military matters.

Beijing and Washington promised to expand dialogue on AI safety and between the countries' militaries while also cutting tariffs on about $30 billion (€26.3 billion) of "non-sensitive goods."

The pledges follow the three-day summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in the US.

US President Trump described the summit in an online post as "one of Friendship, Strength, and Success" for both nations.

China's President Xi was more constrained, saying the two sides agree on "strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."

Beijing and Washington to improve military communication

On Saturday, with Xi back in Beijing, China said the two sides agreed to a mutual tariff reduction on roughly $30 billion of "non-essential" goods. This applies to exports such as agricultural products or holiday decorations.

The Chinese statement also confirmed that the two side will be setting up a "communication channel" for AI incidents.

"Artificial intelligence technologies are continuously developing, all parties can strengthen exchanges, discuss in-depth and seek consensus in light of the latest situation," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said.

A new round of AI-focused dialogue is due to be held in November.

The two nations will also accelerate their work on military crisis communications, Beijing said, without providing details.

Xi to travel to the US again in December

The US had previously announced that Beijing and Washington agreed to extend their "trade truce" agreed by Trump and Xi in Busan last October. The agreement, which saw China suspending its controls on rare earths and the US cutting back on some of its tariffs, was due to expire on November 10. According to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the deal will remain in effect until January.

The White House also said the two sides addressed American concerns about rare earths supply "with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels." China also agreed to import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the US in 2027 and 2028, according to the Trump administration.

While Donald Trump confirmed the Iran war was also on the agenda during the US talks, no major breakthroughs were reported on the issue. However, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said both sides agreed that Iran should not have nuclear weapons, and no country should impose transit tolls on international waterways, in reference to the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump and Xi are due to meet twice more by the end of the year, with Trump expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ​summit in China in November and Xi expected back in the US for a G20 summit in December, which is due to be hosted in Trump's National Doral Miami golf club.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Trump rejects Iran proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump says he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and put an end to hostilities. "I'd like to make a deal, too," he said. "But that deal would not be acceptable."
entries.content:
Iran

Trump rejects Iran proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz

September 26, 2026

US President Donald Trump says he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and put an end to hostilities. "I'd like to make a deal, too," he said. "But that deal would not be acceptable."

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and bring about an end to hostilities.

"I reject their proposal ... I rejected their deal," Trump told reporters at the White House in Washington, DC.

Iran had proposed an initiative aimed at reopening the strategic waterway at the UN General Assembly in New York, which it said could put an end to fighting within seven days.

Tehran said the proposal had been transmitted to Washington via Qatari mediators.

What did Trump say?

"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," said Trump, claiming: "We're winning tremendously."

Earlier, a US official had told Reuters that discussions with Iran, conducted through mediators, were "positive and constructive."

But the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was skeptical that Tehran would meet his demands. He reportedly told staff that a renewed bombing ‌campaign ​is likely following the November US midterm elections.

"They want to make a deal and I think that's fine," said Trump. "What they want to do is ​immediately open the Hormuz Strait ... because they have no money coming in, because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait."

Iranian ports are currently under a US blockade as Washington attempts to pressure Tehran into lifting its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. The key waterway remains largely closed to international shipping despite claims by Trump that the US is control of it.

"I'd like to make a deal, too," said Trump. "But that deal would not be acceptable."

Hours earlier, the US President had posted an image on social media calling the Strait of Hormuz the "Trump Strait."

Strait of Hormuz: What was the Iranian proposal?

Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who was on his way back to Tehran after attending the UN General Assembly in New York, told CBS News the proposal had been developed "in coordination" with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.

He said the process would have begun "from the very day they accept it."

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who met with Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff earlier in the week, said the plan had foreseen a cessation of all hostilities across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, with the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened on the seventh day of the truce.

He said the conditions were the same as those laid out in a memorandum of understanding signed with the US earlier this year, which called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Paris: Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass before huge crowd
entries.summary: The pope addressed around 700,000 people during a Mass at the Place de la Concorde, near the Champs-Elysees. Leo XIV is on a four-day visit to France.
entries.content:
France

Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass before huge Paris crowd

September 26, 2026

The pope addressed around 700,000 people during a Mass at the Place de la Concorde, near the Champs-Elysees. Leo XIV is on a four-day visit to France.

Pope Leo XIV on Saturday celebrated Mass for hundreds of thousands of worshippers in central Paris.

The Vatican said some 700,000 people were in attendance for the open-air service at the Place de la Concorde, near the Champs-Elysees.

What do we know about the Mass?

The Mass began mid-afternoon after the pontiff traveled down the French capital's iconic avenue in his popemobile, cheered by the faithful lining the route.

News agencies described how the crowd stretched ‌2.2 kilometers (1.4 miles) across ⁠central ⁠Paris, with many waving white and yellow flags and pressing against security barriers for a glimpse of the pontiff.

At the Mass site, a huge white canopy was erected to serve as a makeshift altar for Leo to deliver his service, which lasted an hour and half.

Dozens of screens were installed to allow worshippers to follow the proceedings.

In his homily, Leo asked worshippers not to keep their faith to themselves. He urged Catholics to find happiness in faith, not material things.

"Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied," he said. "From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France."

"Only God can fill the emptiness within us," said the pope.

Crowds began queuing hours before the service began, with many parents and children among those hoping to catch a glimpse of the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.

"It's a big event; we've come to share the Christian fervour," teacher Sylvie Leclerc told the AFP news agency.

"You don't hear much from us Catholics, but now we're going to make some noise! But to proclaim love, peace, joy," she added.

Earlier on Saturday, the pope visited a social center and later met with adults who had recently been baptized.

Leo's first trip to France as pope

Pope Leo is on a four-day visit to France that will see him travel to Lourdes and Metz, as well as Paris. It's his first visit to France since becoming pope last year.

On Friday, around 300,000 people gathered to see the pontiff as he waved from his popemobile on the way to the restored Notre Dame Cathedral, which had to be restored after a devastating fire in 2019.

French President Emmanuel Macron did not appear at the Mass. However, far-right leader Marine Le Pen and centrist Edouard Philippe have confirmed their attendance.

Edited by: Sean Sinico, Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
entries.summary: Drone explosions, airspace violations, arson attacks: Poland, Romania, and Moldova are now regularly targeted in Russian attacks against Ukraine. More governments are calling these attacks deliberate acts of aggression.
entries.content:
Europe

Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe

September 26, 2026

Drone explosions, airspace violations, arson attacks: Poland, Romania, and Moldova are now regularly targeted in Russian attacks against Ukraine. More governments are calling these attacks deliberate acts of aggression.

Just a few months ago, Russia's war was an distant reality for many people in Europe outside of Ukraine. If Russian drones occasionally entered the airspace of countries like Poland or Romania, even official statements seemed strangely dismissive and abstract. Even after a Russian drone struck a high-rise apartment building in the eastern Romanian city of Galati in late May this year, many EU and NATO representatives hesitated to accuse Russia of intentional action. At most, there was discussion of hybrid warfare.

The situation has changed radically since the summer. Drone overflights have become almost daily in certain parts of central and southeastern Europe, and there have even been crashes and explosions, particularly in countries bordering Ukraine. Alerts are becoming more frequent, with authorities increasingly having to close airspace or suspend operations at airports, as unauthorized flights are detected. Russia has been bombing border crossings, infrastructure and trains in Ukraine, but very close to other borders. Acts of sabotage are also increasingly common.

For the Baltic states, Poland, Moldova and Romania in particular, the war has long ceased to be "hybrid." More and more, politicians in these countries are saying that Russia is acting deliberately.

Drones violate Moldovan and Romanian airspace

This became evident this week in an unprecedented manner. Moldova recorded four drones entering Moldovan airspace, two of which exploded in Moldovan territory. Wreckage of another was also found. The country's northern airspace was closed temporarily.

Two drones also violated Romanian airspace; with one crashing near the northern town of Solca. A nearby border crossing with Ukraine a few dozen kilometers away was closed as a result. NATO aircraft were scrambled near the Danube Delta.

The scrambling of NATO aircraft has become more common in response to Russian air attacks in Ukraine.

In Poland, NATO fighter jets were scrambled twice in response to Russian attacks near the border with Ukraine. Two Polish border crossings were evacuated after a fire broke out at a Starlink ground station near the village of Wola Krobowska, 40 kilomters (ca. 25 miles) south of the Polish capital Warsaw, on Wednesday night. The station is used to route internet traffic through Poland to Ukraine.

On the same day, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds according to the Polish military.

Polish Prime Minister Tusk says Europe needs to prepare

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke very bluntly in Krakow on Thursday and said that Russia was refining its "disgusting forms of pressure" and Poland must be prepared for them.

Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to exhaust Ukraine by destroying its industrial and energy infrastructure, but he also wants to exhaust Europe," Tusk said. He added that there was a suspicion that the fire at the Starlink ground station had been deliberate.

Earlier this month, Tusk had already warned the Polish parliament that there might be Russian drone and even missile attacks against those who supported Ukraine.

Moldovan President Maia Sandu also reacted very strongly on Thursday, saying that Russia's war was a danger to all of Europe and reasserting Moldova's support for Ukraine.

In Romania, reactions were less clear. Defense Minister Radu Miruta said that not more than a "diplomatic protest" was needed, though he acknowledged that the drone that had crashed in Solca had new technical features, which suggested it could be a newer type of Russian jet-powered drone. 



In New York on Wednesday, in his address to the United Nations General Assembly, Romanian President Nicusor Dan had said: "We are in the fifth year of the illegal, unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression waged on a large scale against Ukraine by a permanent member of the Security Council." He had added that as the "EU member state with the longest border with Ukraine, Romania has directly felt the effects of this war through repeated violations of our airspace."

And he too reasserted support for Ukraine: "We have said it before, and we say it again: Romania will stand with Ukraine and its people, who are acting in legitimate self-defense, for as long as it takes."

Attacks on western Europe from the Mediterranean?

Meanwhile, there is growing speculation that Russia could expand its war to Western Europe. On Thursday, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo published information about a CIA report warning that Russia could be preparing drone attacks on Italy, France and Spain. The attacks could be launched from international waters in the Mediterranean and from vessels that were part of Russia's shadow fleet.

There has been no official confirmation so far. French President Emmanuel Macron said that that the CIA had not informed France of this information, but he did say that the possibility Russia could launch an attack against Europe was "plausible."



At a press conference in Denmark on Thursday, politicians and military officials warned that Russia was expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months. The situation is currently the most serious since the end of the Cold War," said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Germany's FM Wadephul meets Lavrov on UNGA sidelines
entries.summary: It's the first such meeting since Russia launched the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. DW has the latest on day 5 of the UN General Assembly debate.
entries.content:
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 26, 2026

It's the first such meeting since Russia launched the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. DW has the latest on day 5 of the UN General Assembly debate.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul meets Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov on sidelines of the UN General Assembly debate
  • Wadephul addressed the UN later on Saturday and urged regulation on AI
  • India urges de-escalation in regards to Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises
  • Chinese VP Han Zheng slams 'unilateral military actions,' says big countries should follow rules

We are continuing our coverage of the 81st UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Wadephul: Russia's war in Ukraine 'shows contempt' for UN charter

Wadephul: Russia's war in Ukraine 'shows contempt' for UN charter

Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia's war in Ukraine targets the lives of millions of innocent civilians, Ukraine and its culture, as well as the "European peace order."

"It puts vital grain deliveries for millions of people at risk, particularly in Africa, Asia and the Middle East," Wadephul said in his speech to the UN General Assembly, adding that Russia's actions "show contempt" for the UN charter and for the "common order on which we stand."

The minister also said Germany's support with Ukraine was consistent with UN values.

"Today Germany is the largest supporter of Ukraine and its defense against Russian aggression. This aggression has been condemned consistently by an overwhelming majority here in the General Assembly," Wadephul said.

He said Germany would continue to call on Russia to come to the negotiation table.

"I call on every member state to join us in convincing Russia that the future is built at the negotiation table, not on dead bodies in cities and villages," he added.

Prior to his speech, Wadephul met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the UNGA, in the first of such meetings since 2022.

The talks come in the midst of tensions between Berlin and Moscow, after Germany accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulate.

"Wadephul called on the Russian Federation to abandon its dangerous path of escalation vis-a-vis Germany, Europe, and NATO," a German diplomat said of the talks in comments to AFP news agency.

"He made it clear: incidents such as the recent attempted attack in Leipzig or further hybrid assaults would not shake Germany's resolve to support Ukraine, which has come under attack," the diplomat added.

"The German foreign minister condemned Russia's ongoing and increasingly targeted aggression against the Ukrainian civilian population. This attempt to increase pressure does nothing to change Russia's untenable situation: every month, tens of thousands of Russian soldiers die in a hopeless war of positions, while the Russian economy continues to collapse," the diplomat said.

Skip next section Germany calls for AI regulation, urges 'profound' UN reform

Germany calls for AI regulation, urges 'profound' UN reform

Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul opened his UN General Assembly speech by warning about the extraordinary power of artificial intelligence and its implications for the world. He also addressed the erosion of international institutions in a world of rising nationalism.

"When a technology has the power to fundamentally change the world, we need to ask who controls it, who sets the rules, who is accountable," Wadephul said, adding that AI has the potential to upend the economy and "endanger the infrastructure that keeps our societies running."

"AI holds extraordinary promise," Wadephul said. But he warned that a "critical tension" exists when the technology is concentrated in two countries and a few companies. Such power holds great responsibility to humanity, Wadephul said, saying that as power becomes global, so must the responsibilites.

"AI is not waiting for our institutions to catch up, our institutions have to catch up with AI" Wadephul said.

"We need to make sure that tech progress is guided by a framework that we all have a say in shaping," he added, calling effectively for global regulation of AI.

"Germany calls on UN member states to work towards common safety requirements for the most capable models," he said.

On the weakening of UN institutions, Wadephul warned of a UN "under pressure."

"There are great powers that believe that they fare better if they ignore the rules enshrined in the UN charter,"

Wadephul said that "the overwhelming majority of the 193 states represented in this assembly" are harmed when international institutions are under attack.

"If this erosion contitnues, we all stand to lose," he added.

Germany's foreign minister urged for the the new UN Secretary General to lead "a profound process of reform," as the world needs "a functioning UN that plays an active role in conflicts, rather than managing."

"Germany stands up for peace and security," Wadephul said, citing his country's commitment to support Ukraine.

A new nationalism is not the path for nations, Wadephul said, adding that "it would makes our lives narrower, poorer and less secure"

Skip next section India urges de-escalation amid Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises

India urges de-escalation amid Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises

India's Minister for External Affairs, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, addressed the UN General Assembly, urging de-escalation and restraint from those involved in conflicts that have caused disruption to world navigation, in reference to the current crises in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea.

"In a globalized world, the effects of war are felt worldwide," Jaishankar said.

"Countries far from conflicts are being penalized for no fault in this. Those most impacted often have the least say," he added.

Jaishankar also denounced the security of seafarers caught in conflicts.

"We must ensure that the safety and security of shipping and seafarers is never compromised," he said.

Skip next section Saudi Arabia says international community 'absent' in Gulf crisis

Saudi Arabia says international community 'absent' in Gulf crisis

At UN, the Foreign Minister of Saudi Arabia, Prince Faisal bin Farhan al Saud, called for the defense of freedom of navigation in all international waterways.

"The international community has been absent from assuming its responsibilities in confronting all that threatens international peace and security," bin Farhan told the United Nations General Assembly.

The Saudi foreign minister called for the restoration of the Strait of Hormuz to its "pre-28th February status." The US and Israel began their military operations against Iran on that date.

He condemned the fact that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf nations "have been subjected to flagrant Iranian attacks" targeting their security, resources, and civilians.

Saudi FM also denounced Israel's war in Gaza, saying it opposed the "continuing suffering of the Palestinian people."

"We stress that a just and lasting peace can only be achieved through the implementation of a two-state solution and the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital."

Skip next section Russia offers to help with Strait of Hormuz crisis

Russia offers to help with Strait of Hormuz crisis

Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that Moscow can help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region.

"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states, and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov said in his speech to the UNGA.

"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region," he added.

Skip next section Lavrov claims Europe 'thwarts' Ukraine talks

Lavrov claims Europe 'thwarts' Ukraine talks

Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addressed the UNGA, shortly after meeting with his German counterpart Johann Wadephul.

In his speech to the general assembly, Lavrov accused European countries of "doing everything" to thwart talks to help end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

Russia's unprovoked invasion of its neighbor will soon mark its fifth anniversary next February.

"Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the (Donald) Trump administration is interested," he said, referring to the US government and the various rounds of talks it has held with the Russian and Ukrainian government, led by Trump's son in law Jared Kushner and adviser Steve Witkoff.

Skip next section German FM Wadephul meets Russia's Lavrov during UN assembly

German FM Wadephul meets Russia's Lavrov during UN assembly

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov at the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

A correspondent for the Russian Interfax news agency reported Wadephul and Lavrov, followed by aides, shaking hands before the press was asked to leave.

Russian ​Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria ​Zakharova said the meeting took place at the German initiative.

Moscow has been sanctioned by the EU over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine which the Kremlin launched in February 2022.

The last meeting between on this level was held in January of that year, between veteran diplomat Lavrov and Germany's then-top diplomat, Annalena Baerbock, who was on a visit to Moscow.

Lavrov and Wadephul's meeting was held as tensions between Berlin and Moscow have been high in recent weeks.

Germany has accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulate.

Skip next section Moldova PM offers his country as testing ground for AI rules

Moldova PM offers his country as testing ground for AI rules

Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan used part of his time before the General Assembly to present a vision of small nations serving as "regulatory sandboxes" for new technologies.

"Technology is moving faster than regulation almost everywhere, and artificial intelligence is widening that gap," said Tofan, who worked as an investor and businessman before becoming the head of Moldovan government two months ago.

"We want Moldova to become a place where emergent technologies can be tested responsibly through regulatory sandboxes, where regulators learn alongside companies, rules adjust with evidence, and good ideas do not wait years to reach the real economy."

"When an entrepreneur arrives with a technology for which the law has not caught up yet, the answer should not simply be 'There is no rule for this.' It should be 'Let us find a safe way to test it'," he said.

Skip next section China cast itself as source of stability in changing world

China cast itself as source of stability in changing world

Addressing the UN General Assembly, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng called for safeguarding the post-WWII order, saying the world wanted "peace, not war."

"We should turn into action the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, and reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation," Han said.

"Major countries shoulder special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding the rule of law, and doing what's right."

"No matter how international dynamics evolve, China remains unchanged in its pursuit of peace and development, in its dedication to safeguarding fairness and justice and in its commitment to multilateralism," said the Chinese vice president.

"China will join hands with all other countries to build a community with a shared future for humanity, and make the world a better place for all of us."

Skip next section China takes indirect swipes at US over Iran

China takes indirect swipes at US over Iran

Speaking at the UN on Saturday, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng said the world should reject "unilateral military actions that violate the UN charter and circumvent the Security Council authorization," in an apparent reference to the US attack on Iran.

"China holds that the sovereignty and security of the countries in the Middle east, including the Gulf, should be respected, international industrial and supply chains should be kept stable and unimpeded, and global trade should be safeguarded," he said.

In his speech, Han also spoke out against the US blockade of Cuba, albeit without explicitly mentioning the US.

He said China called on "the relevant country" to lift its blockade against Cuba and stop using the threat of force against the island nation.

In regards to Israel and the Palestinians, the Chinese official urged bringing the two-state solution back "on the right track" and "at an early date."

Skip next section Welcome back

Welcome back

Welcome back to DW's coverage of the UN General Assembly Debate in New York City.

On day 5, China and Germany are some of the major countries addressing the event.

Stay tuned for more.

Skip next section We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage

As the fourth day of the 81st UN General Assembly comes to a halt, we are pausing this blog for the night.

Today was another address-packed day, with several small island nations stressing the urgent need to address climate change, as they are most vulnerable to its consequences.

Norway and Sweden stressed the importance of continuing to support the UN, including with funds, as well as making it more representative by giving Africa a permanent seat on the Security Council.

Meanwhile, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took aim at India, rehashing in his address a short-lived conflict between the two countries last year. Sharif said his country faced "external aggression from India under a false pretext," adding that his country's response was "its inherent right of self-defense."

Before the session wrapped, India used its right of reply to address Pakistan's "bizarre remarks," and accuse its neighbor of terrorism. Pakistan was quick to respond, accusing New Delhi of "export[ing] terrorism and violence."

We will be back again tomorrow, when addresses from India, Germany, Russia, China, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Canada, and others are scheduled.

Skip next section Day 4 at UNGA: Egypt, Norway, Sweden, Mexico outline priorities during afternoon session

Day 4 at UNGA: Egypt, Norway, Sweden, Mexico outline priorities during afternoon session

Skip next section Small island states take aim at world leaders for inaction on climate change

Small island states take aim at world leaders for inaction on climate change

The speakers for the small island nations of St. Kitts and Nevis, Samoa and Tonga called to attention the inaction of world leaders on climate change.

The island nations are disproportionately vulnerable to the climate crisis, with the deputy prime minister of Samoa, Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo, calling climate change "the single greatest threat" facing the country and the world.

Molioo stressed the need to scale up climate financing so small island nations weren't the ones bearing the burden of climate change.

Fatafehi Fakafanua, Prime Minister of Tonga, said Pacific leaders have been warning about the climate crisis, with little support for years.

Fakafanua said the question was not whether the world has heard the message of climate change but rather, he asked, "why has it still not acted?"

The deputy prime minister of St. Kitts and Nevis, Geoffrey Hanley, outlined some of the solutions his country has undertaken, such as investing in desalination and improving food security.

Hanley said that small states, who stand most at risk from the consequences of climate change, were still delivering big solutions.

But he said, because no small island state can perpetually adapt to the climate crisis, "adaptation cannot excuse inaction elsewhere."

Skip next section Iran says it gave US 7-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz

Iran says it gave US 7-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz

Iran has given the US a seven-day plan that would involve reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday.

Speaking to reporters at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, Araghchi said the plan was delivered via Qatar and the choice now rests with Washington to meet the conditions Tehran has laid out.

"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," he said.

entries.title: Pakistan: Suicide attack at police stop kills at least 11
entries.summary: The blast was claimed by the Pakistani Taliban, which has stepped up attacks on Pakistani security forces in recent years.
entries.content:
September 26, 2026

The blast was claimed by the Pakistani Taliban, which has stepped up attacks on Pakistani security forces in recent years.

At least 11 people were killed in a suicide bombing in northwestern Pakistan on Saturday, authorities said.

The blast happened just two days after fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan along their southwestern border killed at least 13 members of the Afghan Taliban.

What do we know?

Police said the bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at a roadside police checkpoint in Dera Ismail Khan, the country's 10th largest city.

Dera Ismail Khan sits in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which runs along the border with Afghanistan and has been repeatedly hit by Islamist militant violence.

Around 30 others were wounded in the blast, mostly security personnel and passersby, a police official said.

Emergency teams from Rescue 1122 provided medical ​assistance to ‌the wounded and took them to the hospital, the ​service said.

Police said some of the injured were in a critical condition.

The Pakistani Taliban — Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) — an Islamist militant group that targets the Pakistani state, claimed responsibility in a statement.

Islamist attacks on the rise in Pakistan

Pakistan has experienced a surge in militant attacks in recent years.

Many of them have been claimed by the TTP and the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army, or BLA, a separatist group mainly active in neighboring Balochistan province.

The TTP is aligned with Afghanistan's Taliban, which returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021 when US and NATO troops pulled out.

Pakistan has repeatedly accused Kabul of allowing TTP members to operate from Afghan soil and demanded firmer action to stop cross-border attacks.

The Taliban have denied allowing their territory to be used for attacks.

The rift has sparked cross-border attacks by both countries, with Pakistan carrying out deadly airstrikes it says target militants on Afghan soil.

China, Turkey, Qatar and Saudi Arabia are trying to mediate a lasting peace between the two neighbors.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: German Olympic Committee names Munich as bid city choice
entries.summary: Munich has been voted as the city that will bid for the Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044. Berlin had been in the running but withdrew on Thursday.
entries.content:
September 26, 2026

Munich has been voted as the city that will bid for the Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044. Berlin had been in the running but withdrew on Thursday.

The German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) on Saturday announced it chose Munich as Germany's entry to bid for at least the next three Olympic Summer Games.

Ahead of the vote, former Olympic champion and new Sports Minister Ronald Rauhe said: "We have an international task to fulfill and must enter the race with the city or region that gives Germany the greatest chances internationally. The decision on that is made by sport, and I assume that it will make it with a great deal of responsibility."

Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said the Olympic bid represented a huge opportunity for all of Germany to "show that we are a land of opportunity."

According to the Munich bid, all competitions would take place in Bavaria, except for the football matches which would be played in Stuttgart and the sailing competitions in the northern city of Kiel.

Berlin bowing out created two-horse race

Munich and a Cologne-led bid by the Rhine-Ruhr region were the only two in contention.

As many as 17.6 million tickets could be sold for the Games in Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr, more than ever before at a Games, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia said recently.

Munich was campaigning after two failed bids for the 2018 and 2022 Winter Games and having previously hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics.

Up until Thursday, Berlin had been among the cities in contention, but the city's mayor announced that the city would withdraw from the race.

The withdrawal comes after the socialist Left Party's victory in the German capital's elections last weekend. The party's lead candidate and potential mayor, Elif Eralp, said she did not support Berlin's bid.

Sports minister has sights set on 2040

On Friday, Sports Minister Ronald Rauhe said he would welcome a German Olympic bid for the 2040 Games, with it coinciding with an important historical milestone.

"2040 will mark the 50th anniversary of reunification. Here we could send a great signal that also aligns with the values of the Olympic Games," Rauhe told German news agency dpa ahead of the deciding vote on Saturday.

"Based on my personal history, 2040 would be my favorite date. That has to do with the fact that I'm a Berlin child. As a schoolchild, I experienced what happens to people when a wall falls, when people grow together again, when two population groups that had been separated become a community again,” Rauhe said.

"Ultimately, though, one thing matters above all: bringing the Olympic and Paralympic Games back to our country. No matter when," Rauhe said.

entries.title: Propaganda in Russian schools prepares students to die
entries.summary: The Russian government wants children to learn about patriotism from an early age. DW spoke to students in Siberia about their views on propaganda, the war in Ukraine and their future.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Propaganda in Russian schools prepares students to die

September 26, 2026

The Russian government wants children to learn about patriotism from an early age. DW spoke to students in Siberia about their views on propaganda, the war in Ukraine and their future.

Earlier this year, several schools in Novosibirsk, a city of 1.6 million in southern Siberia, received a textbook on patriotism from the authorities. According to students, with whom DW spoke to on condition of anonymity, in the book the authors urge children to prepare themselves to die for their country. Furthermore, they equate homosexuality with pedophilia and Disney cartoons with pornography, and give instructions on how women should use their "charms." Europeans are described as "thieves, murderers and liars."

The textbook, which provides "materials for spiritual, moral, and patriotic upbringing" is supposed to be used as part of "patriotism lessons" that have been on the curriculum since 2022. Though it is not included on the national list of core curriculum books, the content reflects the Kremlin's intentions to spread propaganda in educational institutions.

'Love always involves sacrifice.'

One of the main topics of the book is the war in Ukraine and the idea that dying for one's country is a blessing is repeated several times: "Love always involves sacrifice," writes one of the authors. "The sacrifice of a defender of the homeland is their life."

Elsewhere in the book, the authors make constant claims that Russia is better than Western countries. They also say that children are "mentally crippled" because of "computer games, Hollywood action films, pornography and Disney cartoons."

They argue that European nations that used to be colonial empires legitimized "murder, lies and plunder" through the conquest and subjugation of new territories. Russia, on the other hand, "never exploited its numerous peoples," they say, but merely improved their living conditions. The book makes no mention of the culture of Indigenous peoples in what is Russia today, or of any religions other than Christianity and "Slavic paganism."

'More cannon fodder'

For Ilya, a 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk who has read the book and whose name has been changed, the idea of dying for his country is anathema. "It's proof that the country wants more cannon fodder," he told DW, adding that "dying for the country" actually meant dying for "the president's interests and ambitions."

He said that a few years ago, he had started watching the videos of Alexei Navalny, the Kremlin critic and opposition leader who died in jail in 2024 "more for fun than for any other reason." He said it was Navalny's 2021 investigation into Russian President Vladimir Putin's Black Sea palace that had first drawn his attention.

But it was when the authorities decided to block access to the US platforms YouTube and Discord that he began to oppose the government. He set up a VPN out of "contrariness" he said, looking for information about other opposition figures and reading the independent media. As he found out more about the cruelty and senselessness of the war, he criticized the government more strongly.

He confirmed that propaganda had become an integral part of the curriculum in the past four years. On top of the "Conversations about Important Things" that take place every Monday morning, there are now also subjects such as "Fundamentals of Homeland Security and Defense." He said that people who have taken part in the war in Ukraine are invited to lessons focusing on students' future and decisions regarding what career path to take.

Even outside of the classroom, students are encouraged to be "patriotic." Ilya said that a student had been reprimanded by the principal for wearing a sweater with a slogan written in English on it. "Young man, do you realize that your sweater has words on it in the language of unfriendly countries?" she reportedly asked him. "A call to the Federal Security Service will take care of that!"

Ilya also recalled that a school assembly held to mark May 9, which commemorates the Soviet Union's victory over Nazi Germany in 1945, the principal and her deputy had compared what is known in Russia as the "Great Patriotic War" to the current war in Ukraine. They had said that Russia would once again be steadfast and emerge victorious.

'I love freedom'

Alexei (name changed), another 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk, told DW that many of his classmates avoided going to "patriotic events." He too said that the blocking of YouTube had made a difference to him. "I looked into why it was blocked," he said. "Because nothing happens by chance. And that's how my interest in politics began." That's when he realized that the authorities wanted to get rid of inconvenient citizens and suppress free speech. "I love freedom, so it was hard," he said.

Ilya thinks that most students don't take the propaganda seriously. "On the one hand, we laugh about it in class, at least my friends do," he said. "On the other, we don't care. Some simply don't listen. We're very good at being quiet and not talking much about it,"

Dima Zicer is an educator and the author of the Russian-language podcast "Love, Don't Discipline" who moved to Estonia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. He told DW that "many students are happy to be part of a pro-Putin majority that doesn't think about things, according to the principle: 'We'll crush them all; we're stronger than everyone else. Everyone will be scared of us.'"

He said that there was no statistical data to back his argument, but he said that he had drawn his conclusions from his extensive experience working with Russian children, as well as his communication with parents. He said that these often only became aware of how serious the situation was when their children started saying things such as "We'll crush them" or "Putin is great," as well as talking about supposed Nazis and fascists in Ukraine.

Alexei and Ilya, who think differently and want the war in Ukraine to end, are worried about the unstable situation in Russia. They want to leave the country after graduating.

This article was originally published in Russian.
